title: Pick it up and read
author: Augustine
setting: A garden in Milan, late summer AD 386

edition.name: Augustine, Confessiones, edited by Pius Knöll, Corpus scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Latinorum (CSEL) 33 (Prague, Vienna, Leipzig: F. Tempsky / G. Freytag, 1896), public domain; the Open Greek and Latin / University of Leipzig TEI text (csel-dev, stoa0040.stoa001.opp-lat1, CC BY-SA 4.0), whose header credits "Pius Knöll", "F. Tempsky", "1896"
edition.section: Confessiones 8.12.29, the first two sentences (CSEL 33, p. 194)

source_text: Dicebam haec et flebam amarissima contritione cordis mei. et ecce audio uocem de diuina domo cum cantu dicentis et crebro repetentis quasi pueri an puellae, nescio: "tolle lege, tolle lege".
excerpt_note: The first two sentences of 8.12.29. Knöll writes u for consonantal v (uocem = vocem, diuina = divina) and prints divina from one manuscript (the Sessorianus), where the other manuscripts and earlier editions read vicina (F has vicino); the gloss shows both. The digital text marks its first tolle as an OCR error ("toIIe"); the printed edition reads tolle, as given here.

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: uōcem, dīuīnā: macrons follow vōx and dīvīnus; the u is the edition's spelling of consonantal v.
crēbrō: long ē and ō (adverb from crēber); not machine-checked.
contrītiōne: long ī (from contrītus, conterō); not machine-checked.
amārissimā: long ā in the second syllable, as in amārus; not machine-checked.

translation: I was saying these things and weeping in the bitterest crushing of my heart. And suddenly I hear, from the divine house, a voice of someone chanting and repeating again and again, like a boy or a girl, I do not know which: "Pick it up, read; pick it up, read."
translation_note: Most manuscripts read de vicina domo, "from the house next door"; Knöll's divina gives "from the divine house". tolle lege has no object: "pick up, read" (Augustine took it as "pick up the book and read"). The present audio after past tenses is a vivid present.

essay.t: In the late summer of 386 Augustine, then imperial professor of rhetoric at Milan, sat in a garden there in deep crisis.
He wrote the Confessions later, about 400.
In Book 8 he describes the garden of the house where he was lodging, which he and his friend Alypius could use because the owner did not live there.
Under a fig tree he threw himself down and wept, asking how long, tomorrow and tomorrow, why not now.
Then he heard a voice chanting and repeating tolle lege, as of a boy or a girl, he could not tell which.

He tried to remember whether children used such words in some game and could not, so he took it as a divine command to open the book and read the first passage he found, recalling that Antony had taken a Gospel reading he happened upon as addressed to himself.
He opened the book of the apostle Paul and read Romans 13:13-14: not in revelling and drunkenness, not in lust and wantonness, not in strife and envy, but put on the Lord Jesus Christ ...
At once, he writes, all the darkness of doubt fled.
He was baptized by Ambrose in Milan at Easter 387.
Was there a child at all?

Pierre Courcelle argued that the scene is a literary construction, reading even the neighbouring house as the heavenly one, so that the voice is no real child's; Karl Gross, writing in 1954, summarized and rejected this, defending the account as historical testimony.
As early support Courcelle cited a reading found only in the Codex Sessorianus, de divina domo, "from the divine house", where the other manuscripts have de vicina domo, "from the house next door".
Knöll's edition, used here, prints divina; Gross reports that Theiler called the reading nonsensical and that Courcelle later relied on it less.
Augustine himself flags the uncertainty: he could not tell whether the voice was a boy's or a girl's, and he could recall no game that used the words.

questions.q: What did Augustine read when he opened the book?
options: A letter written to him by Ambrose

questions.q: Which reading, found only in the Codex Sessorianus, did Courcelle first cite?
options: de divina domo, "from the divine house"
de vicina domo, "from the house next door"
de summa domo, "from the top of the house"
de caelesti domo, "from the heavenly house"

questions.q: Why did Augustine first hesitate over the words?
options: He tried to recall a children's game that used them
He did not understand the Latin of the words
Alypius told him to ignore the voice entirely
He thought the words were spoken in Greek
